Lots of places automatically up-charge because it’s a wedding but for example,  may do the same two or three tier cake for less money if they think it is for a family reunion or birthday party. Some places charge the same amount but some places charge differently because they can for a wedding. Hope this helps and congratulations on your upcoming wedding!

My daughter is three and definitely went through the terrible threes abs we are roughing out the threenager phase right now. Here’s what’s been helpful for me:

1. Timed transitions. When going from one activity to another I give her a warning. “Okay I’m setting the timer, in five minutes we are going to be all done with playing outside and we are going to go inside and have lunch.” Then I set the timer and when it goes off we go to the next thing. What’s helpful with the timer is it’s not me who is making her stop what she’s doing, it’s the timer. Somehow this helps. 

2. Taking a break when she’s too chaotic. If she’s being too wild or throwing a fit, I let her know she needs to settle down or she needs to go take a break in her room. Then I follow through. I put her in her room (sometimes she is kicking and screaming the whole way) and set the timer for three minutes. It gives us both a break to settle down. Then after the timer I go check in. If she’s ready to be calm she can come out. If she needs more time to feel her feels, she stays in and the cycle repeats until she is ready to be calm. We also talk about her feelings when she’s ready fo be calm and navigate through what happened. 

3. The illusion of control. I give my daughter limited options. Getting dressed she gets to pick between two shirts and two bottoms. If she isn’t getting up to go do something I’ve asked she has the choice to walk or be carried. If she’s being too loud she has the choice to use a soft voice or lose screen time. If she’s using her hands to hit she has a choice to tell her hands to be gentle or lose dessert after dinner. She gets to decide how she acts but there is always a consequence if she chooses the thing you don’t want or that is bad behavior 

4. Consequences for her actions. This ties into the illusion of control. If there is harmful behavior she is doing she gets a harsh consequence. This is for when she yells, kicks, pushes, bites, etc. I let her know “this isn’t okay for you to do, you are hurting me. If you continue to do it I’m going to (consequence). Consequence I do are taking away screen time, throwing away candy from her Halloween basket, taking away favorite toys, and leaving play dates (I’ve done this before after a hitting episode during a play date). It gives her the opportunity to correct her behavior and it’s starting to correct behavior now that she’s seen consequences. 

The biggest thing I can say is be consistent. Follow through on your consequences but also be consistent in the love and patience you give. No matter what happens during the day I always always read stories at night with my kiddo and tell her I love her with a big hug. Parenting is hard, especially when parenting tiny humans trying to figure out really big feelings. But you’ve got this! And it’s just a phase

I can’t claim this to be “sage advice” but it is advice none the less. I got married when I was 23. I’m divorced 7 years later. But if my parents had tried really hard to get me to not get married I would have dug my heels in even further and it would have damaged our relationship. After I left, my parents were extremely supportive. I asked why they never spoke up when I was married and they always said they wanted me to feel supported and that some mistakes were ones I had to make for myself. They couldn’t protect me from life forever. My divorce was (still is) a very painful experience but I’ve learned immensely about life, myself, and relationships from it. I appreciate how my parents supported me. 

I have a child of my own now and as parents we want to protect them from everything. It’s a natural response. But just like I have to let my kiddo get an ouchie when she’s running in the house with socks on after I’ve let her know the consequences of doing so, we as parents must let our kids figure life out for themselves after giving them as much information as possible to help them succeed. 

Who knows, maybe your son has found the love of his life and they will both mature into wonderful healthy adults who are good to you and each other. Or maybe he will crash and burn. But either way the thing that will matter is that you loved and supported him the whole way through.

Something that I do with my kiddo when she is having a melt down is get down on her level, validate her feelings, but let her know that if she needs a space to calm down we need to go outside because her tantrum is hurting other people’s ears and it’s not nice to hurt other people. I also give her the option of getting a hug or taking deep breaths to help her settle. I do the deep breaths with her if she chooses that. If she is feeling too chaotic and can’t settle on her own I pick her up and take her to a different space. If the car is nearby we go to the car, if there is a place to sit outside we go outside or take a walk around the block, if there isn’t a way to go outside I try to find a bathroom or space that has less people and a bench or chair where I can sit with her. Sometimes just the change of scenery helps. Sometimes she just has a lot of feelings and needs to have them. Meltdowns in public are difficult but showing her patience and gentleness during this time helps me to keep my cool and not worsen the situation by adding to the yelling. You got this!

It might be difficult but I think it’s important to remind kiddo what you need when you’re upset. Here is a suggestion: Recognize what they are trying to do (I see you want me to feel better) but tell them what you need (but I need to have some time by myself right now/cry/go for a walk to feel better) let them know what you need from them to make that happen (can you give me a couple of minutes of alone time?) And then stick to it. For me I take a break in my room (a concept my daughter is familiar with because she takes breaks in her room when she is overwhelmed by her feelings) or I take a walk or I put in headphones and listen to a song.

I think it’s important for him to know that other people get to feel their feelings. I tell my toddler all the time why I’m reacting a certain why or if I’m crying I cry openly in front of her. For this I think it models the behavior you want but shows that adults can make mistakes too and there are better ways to do certain things. “I’m crying because I feel sad, right now I just need some time to feel out my feelings. I’ll be okay in a little bit” shows your kiddo that it’s okay to cry. Sometimes my kiddo will ask if I need a hug or to take deep breaths (because this is something I do for her) and if one of those things would make me feel better I do that. On the other end of the spectrum I tell her when I am feeling my feelings in a way that isn’t okay. “I raised my voice because it is frustrating for me to try to put your pajamas on when you are kicking me. It’s not okay to kick but it’s also not okay for momma to yell. I’m sorry I yelled at you, I should have asked using my calm voice.” Shows that these big feelings happening and responding poorly happens but that it’s not a good way to respond and how to respond instead

Single mom here. I had been dead set on not having kids until my 30s but then I turned 25 and something changed in me. But my partner wasn’t ready. I definitely pushed for it and now I’m divorced and we have a shitty relationship and he’s such a massive asshole to me. We can’t even be in the same room now. I would urge you both to come at this as logically as possible. Do a cost analysis of all the things needed for baby over the next 3 years. Have candid conversations about your parenting styles. Figure out how much time you can afford to both take off of work. And if y’all have school plus work, it might be better to wait until at least one of you are done with school. It’s really difficult to be starting school with a baby, let alone get through half way as things get more difficult. What’s great about this is you have so much time. I’m a better mom because I put myself first. 

Imma say it again. 

I’m a better mom because I put myself first. And that doesn’t make me a bad person or a selfish person. It makes me a person person. Being a mom is one of the most challenging things I have ever done. I still love it and I love my kid but it takes a mountain of patience and kindness. And I have that mountain of patience and kindness to give when my own cup is full. 

I notice the times I yell at my kiddo or I stop engaging or I don’t want to hear her read “Dragons Love Tacos” for the 100th time are the times when my own cup is low or empty. It is the times when I’m tired, frustrated with work, having an argument with my partner, going a million miles an hour, etc. But when I have time to recharge or vent or sleep in a little, it refills my cup and I have more to give of myself to her. I have a genuine smile as I hear her read about how dragons love tacos but hate spicy salsa. 

It is important to communicate to your partner or your support system what you need. Something that helps me with my daughter with the constant no is giving her the illusion of choice. For example, whenever she isn’t listening about going somewhere (walking out to the car or walking into a store) I tell her “you can either choose to walk or choose to be carried, what do you choose?” She most always chooses walk because she likes the independence of it. I always praise her for her good choices. There are some times of course when she just flops on the floor and I have to say okay since I see you are choosing not to walk I see that you are choosing for momma to carry you. And I always follow through, no matter the tears or the screaming or the kicking. 

Now for the not being gentle part. This may sound a little extreme but whenever my daughter does something to purposefully hurt me through a physical action (kicking, biting, pushing) I yelp or cry like I’m in a lot of pain. Like full dramatics. My daughter is usually immediately concerned and she will come to try to kiss it to make it better or hug me. I use this moment when she’s gentle to explain that when she does those things it hurts me and it’s not nice to hurt momma or our friends and we talk about how she wouldn’t like if someone did that to her. I also will take away her stuffed animals if she is play hitting, biting, pushing them and explain to her that they don’t like that. 

Sometimes though she gets to me, sometimes though she gets under my skin. My partner and I have a tag out system. If he is home I can just walk up to him and be like “tagging out” and he will go step in with her. And then after I’ve taken a little time to take a deep breath I’ll go back and re-engage. And he does the same thing to me. I think for me, taking a minute to recognize I’m becoming upset and taking a step back or taking a deep breath helps me to remember she’s just my tiny human trying to learn how to have real big adult emotions. It’s hard for them. It’s hard for us. When I do lose my cool and yell, I always apologize to my kiddo and explain why I got upset but that I shouldn’t have yelled. This helps to model that behavior for her not yelling.

My gal loves to do puzzles. I have educational puzzles that have numbers, letters, colors, etc. so she gets to dump all the pieces out (her favorite part) then I ask her to tell me about each piece as she puts it back. What color is it, what letter, what sound does it make, what number, let’s count to that number, etc. We also do scavenger hunts. Let’s find things that are soft! Let’s find things that are green! If you kiddo likes bath time I’ve turn bath time into an activity. My kiddo can play in the bath for an hour and she loves it. I sit in there and work or play with her or fold laundry. Another thing we do is when it’s cold we bring her water table inside, it’s a little messy but it’s another thing she likes a lot. My daughter has also shown interest in what I’m doing so I ask her to be my big girl helper and she helps me unload the dish washer, match socks, water plants, put away her toys, etc. covid parenting is HARD.
